books.section: Topic 3.10 Shaping the New Republic, A. Spain and Great Britain Challenge American Growth

primary_sources: Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation between the United States and Great Britain (Jay’s Treaty), signed November 19, 1794
Treaty of San Lorenzo (Pinckney’s Treaty), October 27, 1795
George Washington, Proclamation on the Whiskey Rebellion (August 7, 1794)
Frederick Kemmelmeyer (attributed), Washington Reviewing the Western Army at Fort Cumberland, Maryland (after 1795)

source: original; documents viewed before writing — all pre-1930 public-domain sources.
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the new federal government established its authority in the period 1789–1800.

documents.title: George Washington, Neutrality Proclamation
documents.source: Paraphrased from George Washington, Neutrality Proclamation, April 22, 1793. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Washington’s own declaration as France and Britain went to war, showing the president setting foreign policy.
documents.text: Paraphrase: With France and Great Britain at war, the United States would be friendly and impartial toward both sides and would not take part in the fighting.

documents.title: Jay’s Treaty (Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation)
documents.source: Paraphrased from the Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation between the United States and Great Britain, signed November 19, 1794; ratified 1795. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The treaty Washington sent John Jay to negotiate, showing what the new government could and could not win from Britain.
documents.text: Paraphrase: Great Britain agreed to leave its forts in the American Northwest within eighteen months. American merchants got only limited trading rights in the British West Indies, and Britain agreed to compensate merchants for cargoes its ships had seized, through a commission that settled the claims.

documents.title: Pinckney’s Treaty (Treaty of San Lorenzo)
documents.source: Paraphrased from the Treaty of San Lorenzo (Pinckney’s Treaty), signed October 27, 1795. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The treaty with Spain, showing the government settling a border and winning use of the Mississippi.
documents.text: Paraphrase: Spain agreed to open the Mississippi River to American shipping and to set the boundary between the United States and Spanish Florida, settling disputes that had lingered since the Treaty of Paris of 1783.

documents.title: George Washington, Proclamation on the Whiskey Rebellion
documents.source: Paraphrased from George Washington, Proclamation on the Whiskey Rebellion, August 7, 1794. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Washington’s proclamation to the western counties, showing the president calling resistance to the laws an attack on the government itself.
documents.text: Paraphrase: Washington declared that the opposition to the laws in the western counties of Pennsylvania amounted to levying war against the United States, and he called on the militia of four states to put the rebellion down.

documents.title: Washington Reviewing the Western Army at Fort Cumberland, Maryland
documents.source: Washington Reviewing the Western Army at Fort Cumberland, Maryland, attributed to Frederick Kemmelmeyer, after 1795, Metropolitan Museum of Art 63.201.2. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A painting of Washington on horseback before the army, showing the president leading troops in person.
documents.text: The painting shows George Washington on a white horse reviewing the Western Army at Fort Cumberland, Maryland: long ranks of soldiers in blue coats with a cannon at the left and mountains behind them.

documents.title: George Washington, Farewell Address
documents.source: George Washington, Farewell Address, published September 19, 1796. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Washington’s advice as he left office, showing the limits he set on the nation’s foreign ties.
documents.text: “It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world.”

documents.title: James Madison, Virginia Resolution
documents.source: James Madison, Virginia Resolution, December 24, 1798. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Madison’s claim for the states, showing that the government’s authority was still contested from within.
documents.text: “In case of a deliberate, palpable, and dangerous exercise of other powers, not granted by the said compact, the states who are parties thereto, have the right, and are in duty bound, to interpose for arresting the progress of the evil.”

figures.caption: Washington reviewing the Western Army at Fort Cumberland, Maryland, attributed to Frederick Kemmelmeyer, after 1795
figures.alt: Painting of George Washington on a white horse, pointing toward long ranks of soldiers in blue coats with a cannon at the left, mountains behind them

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the new federal government established its authority in the period 1789–1800, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the weakness of the government under the Articles of Confederation, the fear of distant authority after British rule, or the wars between France and Britain in the 1790s.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument about the federal government’s authority.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents showing both the government’s authority and its limits.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as Hamilton’s financial program and the national bank, the Judiciary Act of 1789, the Alien and Sedition Acts, or the election of 1800.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument, such as Washington speaking as president to the whole nation, the painting showing the president as a commander, or Madison writing to defend the states against the Sedition Act.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document’s author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing that the government’s authority grew at home while it stayed limited abroad, or that the same decade that proved federal power also produced the first claims that states could defy it.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The new federal government established its authority to a great extent, because it enforced its laws at home, settled its borders and trade abroad, and set the precedents of the presidency, though its authority stayed limited by British and French power and by the states’ claim to judge federal laws.
Context: Under the Articles the national government could not tax, raise troops, or enforce its laws, and Shays’s Rebellion had to be put down by a privately paid militia, so the Constitution’s government had to prove it could act.
Authority at home: Document 4 shows Washington calling resistance to the whiskey tax levying war against the United States and calling out the militia of four states, and Document 5 shows him on horseback reviewing that army, so the government enforced its tax law with force.
Authority abroad, settled borders: Document 3 shows Spain opening the Mississippi to American shipping and setting the Florida boundary, and Document 2 shows Britain agreeing to leave its western forts, so the government settled the disputes left over from 1783.
Authority abroad, limited gains: Document 2 also shows Britain compensating merchants for seized cargoes only through a commission and giving only limited trade, and Document 1 shows the United States declaring itself neutral rather than choosing a side, so the government avoided war it could not afford.
Precedents: Document 6 shows Washington advising the nation to steer clear of permanent alliances, setting a rule for foreign policy, and his two terms set the example for the presidency itself.
The limit within: Document 7 shows Madison claiming the states could interpose against unconstitutional federal laws, so the government’s authority was challenged from inside even as it grew.
Beyond the documents: Hamilton’s financial program and the national bank gave the government money and credit, the Judiciary Act of 1789 built the federal courts, and the election of 1800 passed power peacefully between rival parties.
Complexity: The government’s authority was real but uneven, because it could march an army into Pennsylvania and settle a border with Spain, yet it could not stop British seizures at sea or silence the claim that a state could defy its laws.
